newsitem.title: USA: Ford CEO Trotman agrees to stay until 2000.
newsitem.headline: Ford CEO Trotman agrees to stay until 2000.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. Chairman Alex Trotman on Thursday accepted a board request to stay on until 2000 in a move aimed at allowing enough time for his ambitious cost-cutting initiatives to take hold.

The board's request that he stay until Jan. 1, 2000, came at Trotman's annual performance review, the company said. In a statement, Ford said the board is "very supportive of Trotman and the entire Ford management team and the direction in which it is leading the company."
The board also believes the "major changes" being made in Ford's operating processes would benefit from continuing stability of its management team, the company said.

Trotman launched Ford 2000, a sweeping reorganization of the automaker's product development processes aimed at slashing costs, in January 1995. Under the programme, Ford dismantled its traditional regional development centres in North America and Europe and set up five centres organised around vehicle types.

Last October, the company refined the initiative and reduced the number of centres to three as part of a management shakeup in which it named Jacques Nasser the new head of its core automotive operations. Nasser replaced Edward Hagenlocker, who was named vice chairman.

Ford has also stepped up its cost-cutting moves in the United States and Europe in an effort to meet a net automotive profit margin of 3.3 percent of worldwide sales for 1997. Ford's goal for 2000 is a 5 percent auto profit margin.

"If you look at the task at hand for both Nasser and (Chief Financial Officer) John Devine, the board probably has the view these guys need to be in place a long time to execute all this," said Joseph Phillippi, an analyst at Lehman Brothers.

The board action means Trotman, 63, will be able to stay past his 65th birthday in July 1998, the customary retirement age for senior Ford executives. Trotman, who also holds the titles of president and chief executive officer, was elected chairman Nov. 1, 1993.
Ford spokeswoman Pam Kueber said the company does not require executives to leave at 65, noting that former Chairman Harold "Red" Poling stayed until he was 68.

A published report last September said the board had asked Trotman to remain as chairman and CEO and had bypassed Hagenlocker as its next chairman and CEO. The report also said William Clay Ford Jr., a board member and Ford family member, was a candidate to become the company's next chairman.
Ford denied the report and later issued a statement saying no decisions had been made on Trotman's successor. On Thursday, Kueber said the board made no other executive changes.
"Everything else remains the same," she said.
Kueber declined to speculate on future board actions. But Phillippi said it is conceivable the board could redistribute some of Trotman's titles to anoint a successor before he retires.
Ford's stock closed 87.5 cents lower at $31.75 on the New York Stock Exchange.
